steps.title: Fining and filtration
steps.body: Fining agents bind unwanted particles or compounds, then settle out: bentonite clay removes proteins; egg white or gelatin softens tannins; PVPP removes browning compounds. Filtration physically removes particles; a sterile filter removes yeast and bacteria. Some producers avoid both, arguing they strip flavour.

steps.title: Stability
steps.body: Whites can turn hazy in warm conditions if proteins are unstable; bentonite fixes it. Tartrate crystals form in cold; cold stabilisation chills the wine to about minus 4 degrees so crystals drop out before bottling. Microbial stability matters most for wines with sugar or no malolactic, which are usually sterile filtered.
steps.highlight: Bentonite for protein; cold for tartrates

steps.prompt: What does bentonite remove from white wine?
steps.explanation: Bentonite, a clay, binds proteins that could otherwise cause haze in warm conditions.

steps.title: Bottling
steps.body: Bottling is a risky moment: wine can pick up oxygen or microbes. Lines are sterilised, bottles flushed with inert gas, and dissolved oxygen measured. The closure is chosen for the wine's life: natural cork, technical cork, screw cap or glass. Many wines then rest in bottle before release.

steps.prompt: Which wines are most likely to be sterile filtered?
steps.explanation: Residual sugar and malic acid could feed microbes in the bottle. Dry reds after malolactic are more stable.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fining binds particles; filtration removes them
Bentonite fixes protein haze; cold stabilisation drops tartrates
Bottling must avoid oxygen and microbes
